13080: To purloin something means to steal it, but in a quiet, sneaky, sly way — without force, without confrontation, and often without the victim noticing right away. Think of a pickpocket silently lifting a wallet, not a robber demanding it at gunpoint. The theft is secretive, smooth, and crafty.
What Makes It Different from Just "Steal"

"Steal" is a broad, everyday word. You can steal loudly, violently, impulsively, or calculatedly — the word doesn't judge how.

"Purloin" is more specific. It carries the idea of cunning and stealth. When someone purloins something, they:

  • Take it without drawing attention
  • Often rely on cleverness or opportunity, not force
  • Leave the victim unaware, at least for a while

So every act of purloining is an act of stealing, but not every act of stealing is purloining. A mugger who snatches a bag violently is stealing. A clever spy who slips a confidential document from a desk and replaces it with a copy is purloining.

Purloin has a slightly old-fashioned, formal, and literary quality. You will encounter it far more in books, legal writing, or formal speech than in everyday conversation. Because of this slightly elevated tone, the word is sometimes used with a touch of irony or humor — for example, describing someone sneaking a biscuit from a tin in the same sophisticated language you'd use for a master heist. That contrast creates a gentle comic effect.

It is never used to describe violent theft. It would sound wrong, even absurd, to say someone "purloined" a car by smashing a window and speeding away. The word belongs to the world of quiet, crafty, discreet taking.

Almost anything — but the word is especially well-suited to:

  • Small or portable objects — a key, a letter, a document, a ring, a pen
  • Information or ideas — a secret, a formula, a plan
  • Things of value that can be taken without a struggle — jewelry, money, rare items

The most famous literary use of this word is Edgar Allan Poe's story The Purloined Letter, in which a letter is stolen not by breaking into a safe, but by hiding it in plain sight — a perfect example of the quiet cleverness the word implies.

Purloin sits in an interesting middle ground. It is not a trivial or playful word — it does mean to steal, which is a serious act. However, because of its old-fashioned literary flavor, it is often used for:

  • Petty or small-scale theft (purloining a pen, purloining a slice of cake)
  • Elegant or sophisticated theft (a spy purloining state secrets)

It is almost never used for large-scale, brutal, or violent crimes. You would not say someone "purloined" a bank by threatening people with weapons.

• Someone had purloined the last slice of cake before I got to the kitchen.
  • The student purloined answers from his neighbor's exam paper.
  • Over the years, the dishonest clerk had purloined small amounts of cash from the register.
  • The enemy agent purloined the blueprints from the general's briefcase while he slept.
  • He had a habit of purloining phrases from other writers and presenting them as his own.
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
To purloin = to steal quietly, cleverly, and without confrontation — the word of a pickpocket, a spy, or a sly opportunist, never a brute.
13081:
Purport means the main meaning, substance, or overall message that something conveys — especially a document, statement, letter, or speech.

When you ask "what is the purport of this?" you are essentially asking: "What is this really saying? What is its overall substance and meaning?"

Think of it as the essential meaning that something carries within it — what a piece of writing or speech amounts to, in terms of its central message.
The Subtle But Important Shade of Meaning

Here is where purport becomes interesting and slightly different from simply saying "meaning."

The word often carries a quiet suggestion of "what something claims or appears to mean" — sometimes without you necessarily confirming that it is true, accurate, or fully genuine.

In other words, when you use "purport," you are sometimes reporting the meaning of something at a slight distance — you are saying "this is what it conveys or professes to convey," not necessarily "this is the truth."

This is a delicate but real nuance. It is why lawyers, scholars, and formal writers love this word — it lets them describe what a document says without fully endorsing it.

Imagine your friend hands you a very long, confusing legal letter and asks, "What does it say?"

You would not read every word aloud. Instead, you would say something like: "The overall purport of this letter is that they want you to vacate the apartment by the end of the month."

You are capturing the substance and core message of the letter — not quoting it, not summarising every detail, but conveying what it amounts to in meaning.

These examples move from simple to more nuanced, so you can see the word doing different kinds of work.

  • "She didn't understand the full purport of his words until the next morning."

Here, purport simply means the full meaning and significance of what he said — she didn't grasp it right away.

  • "The purport of the announcement was that the company would be laying off hundreds of workers."

Here, purport means the overall substance and message of the announcement.

  • "He conveyed the purport of the agreement to those who hadn't read it."

Here, he is communicating what the agreement amounts to — its essential meaning — to people who hadn't read it themselves.

  • "The purport of the document is unclear, and the court cannot act on it."

Here, a lawyer or judge is saying that the essential meaning and substance of the document is not clear enough to interpret.

  • "I understand the purport of what you are saying, even if I disagree with it."

Here, purport means the general meaning and thrust of someone's argument. The speaker grasps what the other person is driving at.
How Purport Differs From Similar Words

Since you want complete clarity, here is how purport sits among words that seem close to it:

Purport vs. Meaning
"Meaning" is a broad, everyday word. "Purport" is more formal and specific — it usually refers to the meaning of a communication as a whole (a document, a speech, a message), not just a single word or phrase. You would say the meaning of the word "liberty," but the purport of the letter.

Purport vs. Gist
"Gist" is informal and conversational — "give me the gist of it." Purport is formal and carries more weight. Gist just means a quick summary. Purport implies the substantive, essential meaning — what the thing actually amounts to and conveys.

Purport vs. Substance
These are very close. "Substance" focuses on the real content and material of something. "Purport" focuses on the meaning that it conveys — what it is saying or claiming to say. Purport has slightly more of a communicative and interpretive flavour.

Purport vs. Intent / Purpose
"Intent" and "purpose" are about what someone wanted to achieve — the goal behind something. Purport is about what something means or says, not why someone said it. A document can have a confusing purport but a clear intent, or vice versa.

"Purport" as a noun is a formal word. You will encounter it in legal writing, academic texts, journalism, formal letters, and serious literary prose. It would sound unusual in casual conversation — you would not typically say "what's the purport of your text message?" In everyday speech, people say "meaning," "gist," or "point" instead.

However, when you encounter it in reading, or when you need precision in formal writing, purport is exactly the right word when you want to describe the overall meaning and substance that something conveys or professes to convey.

If you can always remember this, you have truly learned the word:

Purport is the essential meaning and substance that a piece of communication conveys — often with a quiet suggestion that this is what it claims or appears to mean, without necessarily confirming it as true.
13082:
To purport means to claim or appear to be something — but with a built-in hint of doubt about whether that claim is actually true.

When you say something purports to be X, you are saying: "It is presenting itself as X, but I'm not fully convinced — or at least, I'm not vouching for it."

That small cloud of doubt is the soul of this word. Without it, you would just use "is."
Breaking It Down with a Simple Example

Imagine someone hands you a document and says it's a letter signed by the President.

  • If you believe it completely, you say: "This is a letter from the President."
  • If you're not sure — if you're just reporting what the document claims to be — you say: "This letter purports to be from the President."

That second sentence doesn't call the document a fake. It doesn't confirm it's real either. It simply reports the document's own claim while keeping your personal judgment neutral or skeptical. That's exactly what "purport" does — it creates a careful distance between what something says it is and what it actually is.

The verb almost always follows one of these two patterns:

Pattern 1: Something purports to be something.

"The painting purports to be an original Picasso."
"He purports to be a licensed doctor."

Pattern 2: Something purports to do something.

"This pill purports to cure insomnia in three days."
"The report purports to prove that the company was innocent."

Notice that the subject (the thing doing the "purporting") is usually not a person making a loud, active declaration. It's a thing — a document, a product, a piece of evidence, a person's identity — that is simply presenting itself in a certain way. The claim is quieter, more of an appearance than a shout.

You will also frequently see "purport" used in the passive voice:

"He is purported to be one of the richest men in the country."
"The artifact is purported to date back to ancient Egypt."

Here, the meaning shifts slightly toward "it is widely said or believed that…" — like a rumor or general reputation that the speaker doesn't personally confirm. It's still skeptical, but in a softer, more social way: "People say this, but don't hold me to it."
Why the Doubt Is Always There

This is the most important thing to understand: you would never use "purport" when you fully believe the claim.

Compare these two sentences:

❌ "Water purports to be made of hydrogen and oxygen."

That sounds wrong because water is made of hydrogen and oxygen — it's established fact. There's no room for doubt, so "purport" doesn't belong there.

✅ "The ancient text purports to be a lost gospel."

This works perfectly, because whether the text genuinely is a lost gospel is exactly what's in question.

So the word is always pointing at a gap — the gap between what something claims about itself and what the truth might actually be.

These two words are close, but not identical.

"Claim" is typically used for a person actively asserting something with words:

"He claims he was home all night."

"Purport" is more about appearance and presentation — what something seems or pretends to be, whether or not anyone is literally speaking:

"The signature purports to be hers."

A forged signature can't speak, but it presents itself as genuine. That's purporting. Also, "purport" is more formal and tends to carry a slightly stronger shade of skepticism than "claim."

"Purport" is a formal word. You'll encounter it most often in:

  • Legal and court language ("the contract purports to waive all rights")
  • Journalism and investigative writing ("the leaked emails purport to show corruption")
  • Academic and scholarly writing ("the study purports to demonstrate a causal link")

You wouldn't typically use it in casual conversation — you'd sound overly stiff. But in formal writing, it's precise and powerful.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Purport" = to present or claim to be something, with an implied "but I'm not so sure that's true."

It lives in the space between a thing's claim about itself and the unverified reality. Every time you see or use this word, the silent question hanging in the air is: Is it really what it says it is? That question is the heartbeat of the word.
13083:
"Purported" means claimed to be something, but not proven, and often doubted. When you put the word "purported" in front of something, you are saying: "Someone has said this is true, but I am not confirming it — and I may even be skeptical about it."

It is a word that carries a quiet warning: don't take this at face value.

Imagine someone hands you a letter and says, "This is a letter from the President." You haven't verified it. You don't know if it's real. You might even suspect it's fake. So instead of saying "Here is a letter from the President" (which would mean you believe it), you say: "Here is a purported letter from the President."

That one word — purported — tells the listener three things at once:

  1. Someone is making a claim.
  2. The claim has not been proven.
  3. You, the speaker, are keeping your distance from that claim. You are not vouching for it.

This is the most important thing to understand: "purported" almost always carries a shade of doubt or suspicion. It's not a neutral word. When a writer or speaker uses it, they are gently signaling to you, the reader, that you should not simply accept the claim as fact.

For example, if a news article says "the purported mastermind of the robbery was arrested," the journalist is saying: "Police or others claim this person is the mastermind — but this has not been proven in court, and we are not confirming it ourselves." The word protects the journalist from stating something as fact that may turn out to be wrong.
Who makes the claim vs. who uses the word

Here is a subtle but important point. The person using the word "purported" is usually not the one making the original claim. They are reporting someone else's claim while quietly distancing themselves from it.

Think of it this way: the claim belongs to someone else. "Purported" is how you hold it at arm's length, pass it to your audience, and say, "Someone said this — make of it what you will."

"The police found the purported murder weapon."
Someone claims this is the murder weapon. It has not been confirmed by a court or lab. The word "purported" tells you: don't treat this as established fact yet.

"He met with the purported leader of the organization."
Others say this person is the leader, but it's unverified — perhaps the organization is secret, or perhaps there's genuine uncertainty about who runs it.

"She bought a purported antique vase for thousands of dollars."
The seller claimed it was an antique. She believed it or at least paid for it as such. But "purported" hints that this claim may be false — perhaps it's a fake, and she was deceived.

"A man claiming to be a purported expert in nutrition gave a talk at the event."
Someone calls himself an expert, but the speaker using "purported" is signaling they are not convinced of his credentials.

"Purported" does not say the claim is definitely false. It leaves the door open. The antique might genuinely be an antique. The leader might truly be the leader. The murder weapon might really be the murder weapon. "Purported" simply says: we don't know yet, and we're not committing.

However, in practice, when writers use "purported," they often lean toward skepticism. If they fully believed the claim, they would just state it as fact. The very choice of this word is a signal that something feels unverified, untrustworthy, or at least unconfirmed.
How it compares to similar words

Three words behave similarly to "purported," and it helps to understand how they differ:

Alleged is the closest cousin. It also means "claimed but not proven." However, "alleged" is almost exclusively used in legal and criminal contexts — alleged thief, alleged fraud, alleged assault. "Purported" is broader and is used in everyday contexts too, not just legal ones.

Supposed is very similar to "purported" and often interchangeable. However, "supposed" can sometimes just mean "expected to" or "meant to" (as in "you're supposed to call me"), whereas "purported" almost always specifically means "claimed to be." "Purported" also tends to sound slightly more formal and carries a stronger sense of active skepticism.

So-called is the most dismissive of the group. When you say "the so-called expert," you are being openly sarcastic — you are clearly saying you don't believe the claim at all. "Purported" is more neutral and professional; it raises doubt without openly mocking.
Where you will most commonly see this word

You will find "purported" most often in journalism, legal writing, and formal reports. These are fields where accuracy matters enormously, and writers cannot afford to state unverified claims as facts. The word is their tool for reporting what someone else has claimed — honestly, carefully, and without personally endorsing it.

You might also see it in everyday speech when someone is being deliberately careful or cautious about a claim they've heard but don't fully trust.
If you ever need to recall what "purported" means, remember this: it means "claimed to be, but not proven — and probably viewed with some doubt."
13084: "Purposeful" describes a person, action, or approach that has a clear goal or purpose behind it — and is consciously directed toward that goal with focus and determination. Nothing about it is accidental, random, or aimless. It exists to achieve something specific, and it moves toward that something with intent.
The two ways it is used
The word applies in two overlapping ways:
1. Describing a person or their manner

A purposeful person knows what they want. They don't drift through situations waiting for things to happen. They act with a clear sense of where they're headed and why. There is confidence and resolve in how they carry themselves.
2. Describing an action, plan, or effort

A purposeful action is deliberate. It was not done on a whim or by chance. There is a clear reason behind it, and it is designed to produce a specific result.

Both senses share the same heart: a clear goal exists, and everything is consciously aimed at it.
Why "purposeful" is stronger than just "intentional"

Both words involve doing something on purpose, but they differ in depth.

  • Intentional simply means: "I meant to do that." It rules out accidents.
  • Purposeful goes further: "I did that because I know exactly what I'm working toward, and I'm committed to reaching it."

An intentional action avoids accidents. A purposeful action actively drives toward a meaningful goal. The difference is between avoiding randomness and actively pursuing direction.
The feelings the word carries

When you call something purposeful, you're communicating several things at once:

  • Direction — it is pointed at a target, not wandering
  • Deliberateness — nothing happened by chance or on a whim
  • Determination — there is real commitment and resolve behind it
  • Meaningfulness — there is a genuine, worthwhile reason for it
Examples in sentences

"She walked into the room with a purposeful stride."
→ She didn't shuffle in lazily or wander in distracted. The way she walked told everyone: she knows exactly why she's here, and she's ready to act.

"The government took purposeful steps to address the housing crisis."
→ These weren't random policies. They were deliberate moves, clearly designed to solve something specific.

"He lived a purposeful life, dedicating every year to serving others."
→ His life had real direction and meaning. He wasn't just filling time — he was building toward something that mattered.

"Her tone was calm but purposeful."
→ The way she spoke made it clear she had something definite in mind and would see it through.

"The training program was purposeful — each session built on the one before it."
→ Nothing was filler. Every session served a clear role within a larger goal.

"They had a purposeful conversation about the future of the company."
→ This wasn't idle chat. They met with a clear agenda and real things to decide.
The opposite of purposeful

The opposite of purposeful is aimless — drifting without direction, acting without a reason, doing things haphazardly with no goal in mind.

Other contrasting words: purposeless, directionless, unfocused, haphazard, random.

If purposeful is a compass needle locked onto North, aimless is a compass spinning with no fixed point.
Common phrases that use "purposeful"

These are the most natural pairings you'll encounter:

  • Purposeful action — a deliberate, goal-driven act
  • Purposeful stride / walk — walking with clear intent and direction
  • Purposeful life — a life shaped by meaningful goals
  • Purposeful effort — work done with a specific aim
  • Purposeful approach — a focused, goal-oriented way of doing things
  • Purposeful practice — practice that has a real developmental goal, not just going through the motions
One subtle but important point

"Purposeful" doesn't just mean having any goal. It carries a quiet suggestion that the goal is worthwhile — that the purpose behind the action is real and meaningful, not trivial. This is why it often appears with a note of admiration. Calling someone purposeful is almost always a compliment: it says they are not wasting their life or their effort.
In a single sentence
Purposeful = driven by a clear, meaningful goal + acting toward it with focus, deliberateness, and determination — the opposite of aimless, accidental, or random.
13085:
A purse is a small bag designed to hold money — especially coins. Picture a compact, hand-sized pouch, often made of leather or fabric, with a clasp or zipper to keep it shut. You open it, put your coins in, and close it again. This is the oldest and most direct meaning of the word.

From here, the word branches out into several related meanings, all connected by a common thread: money, and the thing that contains it.
1. A small coin pouch — the basic meaning

A purse in this sense is a compact bag for carrying coins and sometimes folded banknotes. It is meant to be small — small enough to fit in your pocket or inside a larger bag.

"She opened her purse and took out some change."

This is the standard meaning in British English. When someone in the UK says "purse," they almost always mean this small money bag.
2. A woman's handbag — the American meaning

In American English, the word has stretched to mean the larger bag a woman carries every day — the kind with handles or a shoulder strap, used for carrying a phone, keys, wallet, makeup, and all sorts of personal things.

"I left my purse on the bus."

Here, the speaker means her entire daily carry bag — not just a small coin pouch.

What Americans call a "purse," the British call a "handbag." This is one of the most well-known vocabulary differences between British and American English. So depending on where you are, or who you are talking to, "purse" can mean a very small coin pouch or a full-sized everyday bag.

In the world of sports — especially boxing, horse racing, and golf — a "purse" refers to the total prize money on offer in a contest.

"The boxing purse for tonight's fight is $5 million."

This means the total prize money for that fight is $5 million. The word is used this way because, historically, prize money was literally placed inside a purse (a bag) and handed to the winner. The physical bag is long gone, but the word stayed.

You will often see the phrase "the public purse" in newspapers and formal writing. It refers to the government's money — the total funds a country's government has available to spend on public services like hospitals, schools, roads, and welfare.

"The new rail project will cost the public purse billions."

This means the government will have to pay a huge amount from its funds.

By the same logic, any organization's total budget can informally be called its "purse":

"The charity has a modest purse for such a large ambition."
5. A collected sum of money given as a gift

In more formal or old-fashioned usage, a "purse" can mean a sum of money gathered by a group of people and presented to someone as a gift, reward, or token of appreciation — as if the money were being placed into a bag and handed over.

"The village presented the retiring doctor with a purse of five hundred pounds."

You are less likely to hear this in everyday casual speech today, but you will encounter it in literature, historical texts, and formal writing.
A key phrase: "Hold the purse strings"

One expression you will see very often is "hold the purse strings" (or "control the purse strings"). It means to be in charge of how money is spent — to be the one who decides what gets funded and what doesn't.

"In that company, the finance director holds the purse strings."
"She controls the purse strings at home."

The image is of someone physically holding the strings of a purse closed — nobody else can get the money out unless that person lets them.

Every meaning of "purse" connects back to the same central idea: money, and something that holds or represents it — whether that's a coin pouch, a woman's handbag that contains one, a prize fund in a sport, a government's treasury, or a gifted sum of money. Once you see this connection, the word never feels scattered or confusing again.
13086:
To purse means to press your lips together tightly so that they form a small, puckered, rounded shape — almost like a tiny knot or a small "o" pulled inward. Think of how a drawstring bag closes when you pull the strings: the opening gathers, tightens, and puckers into a small, bunched circle. When you purse your lips, your mouth does exactly that.

This verb is almost always used with the word lips as its object. You will almost never see "purse" used as a verb without lips being involved.

Picture someone who has just tasted something unpleasant, or someone who is trying very hard not to say what they're thinking. Their lips press together, squeeze inward slightly, and form a tight little round shape — not quite a smile, not quite a frown, but a firm, compact expression. That is pursed lips.

This is where the word gets really interesting and useful. People purse their lips for several reasons, and a good writer or speaker uses this word deliberately because it carries emotional meaning:

Disapproval or annoyance — This is the most common one. When someone hears something they don't like or disagrees strongly, they may purse their lips instead of speaking. It signals silent judgment.

Holding something back — A person might purse their lips to stop themselves from laughing, from crying, or from saying something they shouldn't. The tightness of the lips physically holds things in.

Concentration or deep thought — Sometimes people purse their lips when they are thinking hard about something, especially when working through a difficult decision.

Skepticism or doubt — When someone is not convinced by what you've just said, pursed lips can signal "I'm not sure I believe you."

"Purse" is a transitive verb, meaning it needs an object — and that object is almost always lips. The structure is simple:

  • Subject + pursed + his/her/their lips

It's most often used in the past tense because writers use it to describe a character's reaction in a moment:

"She pursed her lips."

You can also use it as a present participle to show an ongoing action or to modify a noun:

"He sat there, pursing his lips thoughtfully."
"She gave him a pursing-lips kind of look." (informal, rare)

Here are clear, natural examples so you can see the word in action:

  • "The teacher pursed her lips when she saw the messy classroom." — She was displeased but didn't say anything.
  • "He pursed his lips, staring at the math problem for a long time." — Deep concentration.
  • "She pursed her lips to keep from laughing out loud." — Holding back laughter.
  • "My mother pursed her lips when I told her my plan." — Quiet disapproval.
  • "The doctor pursed her lips and nodded slowly before delivering the news." — Thoughtfulness mixed with seriousness.

When you see "pursed lips" in a book or hear someone describe an expression this way, know that it is rarely neutral. Pursed lips almost always mean that a person is feeling something strongly but choosing not to say it outright — whether that's annoyance, doubt, amusement, or deep thought. It is the face of someone holding something inside.

That's the full picture of "purse" as a verb: a tight, puckered pressing of the lips together, loaded with quiet but unmistakable emotion.
13087:
"Pursuant" as an adjective lives almost entirely inside one phrase: "pursuant to." Mastering that two-word phrase is all you need.

"Pursuant to" means in accordance with, following from, or as required or authorized by something. It tells you that an action, decision, or situation exists because of — and in direct obedience or response to — whatever comes right after those two words. That "whatever" is almost always a rule, law, contract, order, or request.

The simplest way to see it in action:

"Pursuant to the contract, payment is due on Friday."

This means: "In accordance with what the contract says — following its terms — payment is due on Friday." The contract is the source. The payment deadline obeys and flows directly from it.

Another example:

"Pursuant to your request, I have attached the report."

This means: "Following your request, and in direct response to it, here is the report." Your request is the source. The attached report is the action that follows from it.

While the core idea stays consistent, "pursuant to" carries slightly different flavors depending on context.

The most common use is "in accordance with / as required by" — when a law, regulation, or agreement is the governing source: "Pursuant to federal law, all employees must be paid minimum wage." Here, the law is the authority, and the requirement follows directly from it.

The second use is "following / in response to" — when an action is a direct follow-up to a request or prior event: "Pursuant to our last conversation, I have drafted the proposal." The conversation prompted the action; the proposal is its direct result.

A third, older and rarer use means "in pursuit of / for the purpose of achieving" something: "measures taken pursuant to peace." This means measures taken with the aim of bringing about peace. You'll rarely encounter this version in modern writing, but it's worth knowing.
How to recognize it and where you'll see it

"Pursuant" is a formal word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. It lives in legal documents, official letters, government notices, business contracts, and formal correspondence. When writing casually, people replace it with simpler alternatives: "as required by the contract," "following your request," "in line with the law." But in formal or legal writing, "pursuant to" is the standard go-to phrase, and you will see it constantly.

Technically, "pursuant" is an adjective because it modifies the subject of a sentence by describing its relationship to something else. In "actions taken pursuant to the agreement," the word "pursuant" describes the actions — it tells you their nature: that they follow from and comply with the agreement. However, in practice, the full phrase "pursuant to" behaves like a preposition — it connects what comes before it (an action or fact) to what comes after it (its source or basis). Don't lose sleep over the grammar label. What matters is how it functions: it links something to the rule, authority, or event that caused or governs it.

Because "pursuant" and "pursuit" share the same root, people sometimes mix up "pursuant to" with "in pursuit of." These are not the same thing in modern usage.

"He acted pursuant to the law" means he acted in accordance with the law — he followed it.

"He acted in pursuit of the criminal" means he chased the criminal.

In modern English, "pursuant to" almost never means physically chasing or hunting. It means following from, obeying, or acting in line with something.

Any time you see "pursuant to" in a sentence, try swapping it with "in accordance with" or "as required by." If the sentence still makes sense, you've read the word correctly. In the vast majority of cases, this substitution will work perfectly, and you'll know exactly what the sentence means.
13088:
Pursue means to go after something — with intention, effort, and persistence over time.

The "going after" can be physical (chasing someone down a street) or it can be mental and emotional (spending years working toward a dream). Both are correct uses of the same word.

The three invisible qualities hidden inside "pursue" are:

  • Direction — you are moving toward something specific
  • Effort — it requires active doing, not passive waiting
  • Continuity — it happens over a period of time, not in a single instant

1. To physically chase or follow someone or something

This is the most literal, visual sense of the word. One thing moves, and you go after it.

The police pursued the suspect through the alley.
The lioness pursued the zebra across the open field.

Here, "pursue" and "chase" are nearly identical. The difference is subtle: "chase" feels more urgent and short-lived, while "pursue" can suggest a longer, more determined effort.

2. To work toward a goal, dream, or ambition

This is the most common and important meaning you will encounter. When someone "pursues" a dream, a career, or success, it means they are consistently putting in effort over time to reach it.

She pursued her dream of becoming a surgeon for over a decade.
He left his home country to pursue a better life.
They pursued excellence in everything they did.

Notice that this meaning lives entirely in the mind and in action — there is no physical chasing involved. Yet it perfectly fits the word because the core idea is still: going after something intentionally, with effort, over time.

3. To continue doing an activity, study, or interest

When you "pursue" a subject or activity, you are actively engaging in it on an ongoing basis — it is something you keep coming back to and developing.

After retiring, he pursued painting as a serious hobby.
The university encouraged her to pursue research in climate science.
She pursued her studies even while working two jobs.

The key here is the word ongoing. You don't "pursue" something you did once. You pursue something you dedicate time and energy to, repeatedly.

4. To keep investigating, discussing, or following up on something

In conversations, meetings, or professional life, "pursue" means to take something further — to not let it drop, but to keep pushing on it.

The detective pursued every lead until she found the truth.
The journalist pursued the story for six months before publishing.
I don't want to pursue this argument any further tonight.
The company decided not to pursue the matter in court.

Here, "pursue" is about sustained attention — you are actively following something through, rather than leaving it unfinished.

5. To seek someone's romantic attention

When a person "pursues" another person romantically, it means they are making persistent, deliberate efforts to attract or win that person's affection.

He had been pursuing her for months before she agreed to a date.
She wasn't interested in being pursued by anyone at that point in her life.
The One Thread That Ties All Meanings Together

No matter which situation you use it in, pursue always carries the same DNA:

Something exists that you want → you move toward it → you keep at it → it takes time and effort.

Whether it is a thief running away, a lifelong dream, a research project, a romantic interest, or an unresolved conversation — the word "pursue" fits whenever that formula applies.

• It is not a one-time action. You don't "pursue" something you did once by accident. The word implies sustained, deliberate effort.
  • It is not passive. You cannot pursue something while sitting still and waiting. Pursuing requires you to actively move toward the thing.
  • It is not the same as "reach" or "achieve." Pursuing is the journey. You pursue a goal; you achieve it (or don't) later.
A Useful Way to Remember It

Think of the word pursue as carrying a built-in image: a person walking steadily forward, eyes fixed on something in the distance, not giving up.

That image — steady, intentional, forward-moving, not stopping — is what the word means in every context it is used.

• pursue a dream / goal / passion / ambition
  • pursue a career / education / degree
  • pursue a matter / case / lead / story
  • pursue someone (romantically or in a chase)
  • pursue happiness / freedom / truth
  • actively / aggressively / relentlessly / vigorously pursue

The word pairs naturally with things that are worth going after and that require sustained effort to reach.

Pursuit means actively going after something. Whether you are physically chasing someone, working hard to achieve a goal, or engaging in a regular activity you love — the word "pursuit" captures the idea of ongoing, directed effort toward something.

Think of it this way: pursuit is never passive. It always involves movement — physical or figurative — toward something.
Meaning 1: Physically Chasing Someone or Something

The most literal sense. When you run after someone to catch them, that is a pursuit.

"The police car raced through the streets in pursuit of the stolen vehicle."

"The cat leaped over the fence, and the dog followed in hot pursuit."

Notice the phrase "in pursuit of" — it simply means "in the act of chasing." "Hot pursuit" is a common expression meaning the chase is immediate and very close — the pursuer is right behind.

This meaning is common in news reports, crime stories, and action scenes. The chaser wants to catch something; the pursuit is the act of trying to do so.
Meaning 2: Trying to Achieve or Obtain Something (Most Common Meaning)

This is the most widely used sense of the word, and it is metaphorical — not physical chasing, but the sustained effort of working toward a goal or an ideal.

"She spent years in the pursuit of knowledge."

"He sacrificed everything in his pursuit of success."

"The pursuit of happiness is a fundamental human desire."

Here, "pursuit" suggests that the thing you want is not yet fully in your hands — you are still striving toward it. It also implies that the process of going after it takes real, ongoing effort.

A very important detail: pursuit here often implies that reaching the goal is not guaranteed. It is the journey of trying, not the moment of arrival. You can spend a lifetime in the pursuit of wisdom without ever feeling you've fully achieved it — and that's the point. The word respects both the effort and the difficulty.

Common patterns you will see:

  • the pursuit of + [abstract noun] → pursuit of truth, pursuit of excellence, pursuit of power, pursuit of justice, pursuit of peace, pursuit of wealth

This is the sense used in one of the most famous phrases in political history: "Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness" — from the American Declaration of Independence. Notice it doesn't say happiness itself is guaranteed, only the pursuit of it.
Meaning 3: A Regular Activity or Hobby

"Pursuit" can also refer to an activity that someone regularly engages in — a hobby, occupation, or pastime. In this sense, it is a slightly formal word for "something you do."

"Reading, painting, and hiking are her favourite pursuits."

"He gave up his outdoor pursuits after the injury."

"Academic pursuits took up most of his time."

This meaning is quite neutral in tone — it simply names what someone spends their time doing. The word carries a subtle implication that the activity requires some effort or engagement (not something mindless), but it doesn't have to be grand or noble. A person's pursuits are simply the activities that define how they spend their time and energy.
The Thread Connecting All Three Meanings

All three meanings share one thing: active, directed effort. Whether you are chasing a thief, chasing a dream, or regularly engaging in something you love — in every case, you are going toward something with energy and intention.

The word never applies to something passive or accidental. You don't stumble into a pursuit — you engage in one.

"Pursuit" is a moderately formal word. It fits naturally in writing, speeches, and thoughtful conversation. In casual speech, people might simply say "going after" or "chasing" something, but when they want to sound more considered or serious, they reach for pursuit.

It also carries a slightly dignified, even noble connotation, especially in Meaning 2. Saying someone is in the pursuit of justice sounds more weighty and sincere than just saying they are trying to get justice. The word respects the effort involved.
